title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
hook: a temple priest at Dakshineswar feeds the Mother's offering to a cat

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams at Durga Puja: the goddess welcomed home as a daughter, then given back to the river. Did you give someone a real welcome, or a real goodbye? Day one thousand three hundred eighty.
screen: `THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: The offering is ready. At Dakshineswar, a temple to Kali on the bank of the Ganges near Calcutta, the food has been cooked and laid out for the Goddess, the offering, and the priest is supposed to present it to her image with the proper rites. Instead, a cat wanders in, and the priest kneels down and feeds the offering to the cat. The temple staff are horrified. Word reaches the owner of the temple. The priest's explanation is simple: he saw the Mother in the cat. Today, that priest: Ramakrishna.
screen: `A KALI TEMPLE ON THE RIVER.` → `THE OFFERING, TO A CAT.` → `I SAW THE MOTHER THERE.`

segments.voice: First, how he got there. In the stories his followers kept, Ramakrishna was a young priest who couldn't treat the image of Kali as a statue. He would cry to her, like a child: Ma, are you real? Why won't you show yourself? He was, by his own telling, close to despair, and the accounts say he reached for the sword that hung in the shrine. In that moment, he said afterward, the walls, the doors, the temple all vanished, and he saw a shining ocean of light, wave after wave, rolling toward him. It was the Mother. Turn it once. After that, the line between the image and the world got thin. That's the cat. He wasn't being careless with the rites. He'd started seeing the Goddess everywhere, so feeding a hungry cat was feeding her. The stories say the owner of the temple, after hearing him out, let him be. Turn it again, because this is where Bengal's two streams meet in one person. The accounts say that later he took up Vaishnava devotion too, and for a time lived in the mood of Radha, longing for Krishna, the way Chaitanya's followers describe. A Shakta priest of Kali, weeping for Krishna. He didn't treat it as switching sides. To him it was the same longing, finding another name. And once more. The visions, he said, can't be put into words. What the stories can show is plainer: a man who talked to God like a child talks to its mother, and who, once he'd seen her, found her in a cat.
screen: `MA, ARE YOU REAL?` · `AN OCEAN OF LIGHT` · `THE MOTHER IN A CAT` · `BOTH STREAMS IN ONE PRIEST`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: seeing through. Sit, and let the breath slow. Open your eyes softly and rest them on one ordinary thing near you: a plant, a cup, an animal, your own hand. Look at it as if it might be more than it seems. Don't force a feeling. Just look, the way you'd look at someone you love who's asleep. Then close your eyes and breathe. If you pray, you can greet God there, in that ordinary thing, by whatever name you use. The bell holds the time.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, Ramakrishna, a priest of Kali at Dakshineswar who saw the Mother in a cat, and who also longed for Krishna like Radha. Today's word.
screen: `BENGAL'S SHAKTA AND VAISHNAVA STREAMS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, feed something hungry, a pet, a bird, a tired friend, and do it as carefully as an offering. Day one thousand three hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Devotees visit the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, where Ramakrishna served as priest, and his sayings and stories are read and retold in Bengali homes and in the monasteries that carry his name.

original.note: Sanskrit: Kali, the dark Mother, worshipped at the Dakshineswar temple where Ramakrishna served.

trapdoor: what you thought: a priest who broke the rules.
what it means: after his vision, he saw the Goddess everywhere, so a hungry cat was the Mother too.
what a scholar hears: his sayings and stories were kept by his disciples; he moved between Shakta and Vaishnava devotion without treating it as a change of side.

sources.ref: Accounts of Ramakrishna by his disciples (e.g. the Kathamrita of Mahendranath Gupta, and Saradananda's Lilaprasanga): the vision of the Mother, the cat, the mood of Radha

notes: Editor pass: hook opener changed for variety; 'what draws people to these stories' (a claim about listeners) replaced with what the stories show.
All of Ramakrishna's words are paraphrased; the standard English translation (Nikhilananda, 1942) is not public domain.

Confirm: the vision of the 'ocean of light' after reaching for the sword in the shrine; the cat fed with the offering; Rani Rasmani (or Mathur Babu) allowing him to continue; his practice of madhura bhava in Radha's mood.
Deliberately omitted: Ramakrishna's practice of other religions and the teaching often summarized as 'as many faiths, so many paths', to keep the day free of comparison between traditions.
'Just north of Calcutta' for Dakshineswar: confirm.
